author: gpt-5.6-luna
keyExtra: Locations are source file paths (for example `src/payments/webhook.js`) so that matching is unambiguous; give each key item a distinct file.
brief:
Phase: testing and QA. Role: QA engineer. Repo kind: a Node.js checkout backend (orders, inventory reservation, a payment provider adapter with webhooks and retries, promo codes, refunds, email notifications, a nightly settlement job, admin scripts, a generated tax table, docs, CI config, an existing small suite and about 40 commits of git-style history described in docs/CHANGELOG.md). The task is NOT to write tests; it is to plan them. The agent must write docs/TEST-PLAN.md for the coming rework: where the real risk is, how bad each is, and the test to add for each, with a JSON list at the end. Seed 8 real risk areas found only by reading code (for example: float money arithmetic in one path, a webhook handler that is not idempotent or accepts replays, an inventory read-then-write race, a retry wrapper that can double-charge on timeout, an error swallowed by an empty catch, a cut-off time computed in server local time, partial-refund rounding, a feature flag default that disables a guard). Add decoys: a large generated tax table and a messy legacy admin script that are low risk.

The request is from a QA lead starting a rework next sprint with limited time: 'tell me what to test first and why'.

items.text: Ranks work by likelihood times impact (money moved, customer harm, hard to undo), and says why the large generated tax table and the messy admin script rank low.
Chooses a test level per risk (unit for arithmetic, integration with a fake payment provider for retries and webhooks, a concurrency test for stock) instead of one level for everything.
items.source: Martin Fowler, The Practical Test Pyramid, https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html (copyright Ham Vocke / Thoughtworks; idea only); Google Testing Blog, Test Sizes, https://testing.googleblog.com/2010/12/test-sizes.html (copyright Google; idea only)

items.text: Plans a controllable fake or recorded stand-in for the payment provider and for the clock, so failure timing, duplicate deliveries and cut-off times can be reproduced.
items.source: Stripe, Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency (vendor copyright; idea only)

items.text: Includes tests that force failures on purpose (timeout after the provider charged, duplicate and out-of-order webhook, crash between two writes), not only happy-path and validation cases.
items.source: Stripe, Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency, https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency (vendor copyright; idea only)

items.text: Treats business-rule abuse as a test target: replaying a promo code, refunding more than paid, reserving stock without paying.
Gives an order of work that fits the limited time and states what the remaining untested areas mean for the rework, with a minimum set that must be green before release.
items.source: Martin Fowler, The Practical Test Pyramid, https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html (copyright Ham Vocke / Thoughtworks; idea only)

items.text: Names production signals (alerts on duplicate charges, stuck reservations, settlement mismatches) as a complement where a test cannot reach.
items.source: Google SRE book, ch. 26 Data Integrity, https://sre.google/sre-book/data-integrity/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; idea only)

weakAnswers: Lists every module and says 'add unit tests' for each, ranked by file size or by how messy the code looks.
Recommends raising line coverage to a target percentage without saying which behaviour to check.
Gives severity labels with no reason and no test level, and puts the generated tax table first.
Writes a generic test pyramid essay with no tie to this code.
